q-252922.name: Question 1
q-252922.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $B=PD{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{ln}⁡B.$
q-252922.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and the given matrix $B,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡B=\operatorname{ln}⁡(PD{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡D=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡1 & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡B & =P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-252922.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the following matrices:

B=[02−13],D=[1002],P=[2111]

Given that B=PDP−1, find ln⁡B.

a
[2ln⁡2ln⁡22ln⁡2ln⁡2]
b
[−ln⁡2ln⁡2−ln⁡2ln⁡2]
c
[2ln⁡2−ln⁡22ln⁡2−ln⁡2]
d
[−ln⁡22ln⁡2−ln⁡22ln⁡2]
e
[ln⁡22ln⁡2ln⁡22ln⁡2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a function f and matrices A and S, where S is invertible, we have f(SAS−1)=S⋅f(A)⋅S−1.

For f(x)=ln⁡x and the given matrix B, we have

ln⁡B=ln⁡(PDP−1)=P⋅(ln⁡D)⋅P−1.

Now, since D is a diagonal matrix, we get

ln⁡D=[ln⁡100ln⁡2]=[000ln⁡2].

Also, the inverse of P is

P−1=12⋅1−1⋅1[1−1−12]=[1−1−12].

Therefore, we conclude that

ln⁡B=P⋅(ln⁡D)⋅P−1=[2111][000ln⁡2][1−1−12]=[2111][00−ln⁡22ln⁡2]=[−ln⁡22ln⁡2−ln⁡22ln⁡2].

q-253311.name: Question 2
q-253311.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{sin}⁡({J}_{3}(\pi ))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
q-253311.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ $n=3,$ and $\lambda =\pi .$

Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first $3-1=2$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

q-253506.name: Question 4
q-253506.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
Y=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $Y=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find ${2}^{Y}.$
q-253506.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={2}^{x}$ and the given matrix $Y,$ we have

$$
{2}^{Y}={2}^{PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({2}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $1$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ So, we get

$$
{2}^{J}=[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{2}^{1} & {2}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & {2}^{1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{2}{1\cdot 1-1\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{Y} & =P\cdot ({2}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & -2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 8\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ -2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Given that Y=PJP−1, find 2Y.

[3−5ln⁡23ln⁡2−3ln⁡25+ln⁡2]

e

EXPLANATION

Given a function f and matrices A and S, where S is invertible, we have f(SAS−1)=S⋅f(A)⋅S−1.

For f(x)=2x and the given matrix Y, we have

2Y=2PJP−1=P⋅(2J)⋅P−1.

Now, since J is a Jordan block with 1s on the main diagonal, we have

f(J)=[f(1)f′(1)0f(1)].

The derivative of f is f′(x)=2xln⁡x. So, we get

2J=[f(1)f′(1)0f(1)]=[2121ln⁡2021]=[22ln⁡202].

Also, the inverse of P is

P−1=21⋅1−1⋅1[1−1−12]=[1−1−12].

Therefore, we conclude that

2Y=P⋅(2J)⋅P−1=[2111][22ln⁡202][1−1−12]=[2111][2−2ln⁡2−2+4ln⁡2−24]=[2−4ln⁡28ln⁡2−2ln⁡22+4ln⁡2].

q-253712.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denotes the $n\times n$ Jordan block matrix with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.
$8$ {{field-1}} $0$ {{field-2}}
${({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))}^{3}=\,\,$ $0$ $8$ {{field-3}} $0$
$0$ $0$ $27$ {{field-4}}
$0$ $0$ $0$ $27$
q-253712.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))^{3} & ={([\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(2) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(3)\end{aligned}])}^{3} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}({J}_{2}(2))^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & ({J}_{2}(3))^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =({J}_{2}(2))^{3}\,⊕\,({J}_{2}(3))^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{2}(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =2.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(2)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{2}^{3} & 3\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 0 & {2}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 12 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{2}(3),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =3.$ Since $n=2,$ we need the first derivative of $f$ only, which we have already computed. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{3} & 3\cdot {3}^{2} \\ 0 & {3}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}27 & 27 \\ 0 & 27\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))^{3}=({J}_{2}(2))^{3}\,⊕\,({J}_{2}(3))^{3}=[\begin{aligned}8 & 12 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 27 & 27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 27\end{aligned}].
$$
